warmup.q: Room 4 is free from 12:00 to 13:00, and two people book it at the same moment. Each one's transaction first runs SELECT ... FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && '[12:00,13:00)' FOR UPDATE, which looks for bookings that overlap that hour and locks any it finds. It finds none, and inserts the new booking. Both run on PostgreSQL with its default settings. What happens?
options: The second SELECT waits for the first transaction's lock, then sees the first booking and refuses
Both inserts commit, and room 4 is booked twice
The second INSERT fails with a serialization error
The second INSERT waits, then fails because the booking already exists
warmup.why: FOR UPDATE locks the rows a query returns, and this query returned none, so there was nothing to lock and nothing to wait for. Neither transaction can see the other's booking before it commits, so both checks pass and both inserts commit. The first option is what a lock on "any booking that would match" would give you, called a predicate lock, and FOR UPDATE isn't one. A rule written into the table, a constraint, would make the second insert fail, but the table has none yet.

sections.h: Two doctors check the rota, and both leave: write skew
sections.html:
Let's start with a rule over rows that do exist. A hospital keeps its rota, the list of who works when, in PostgreSQL, a free database program. The rota is a table called on_call, with one row per doctor per shift. Shift 1201 has two doctors on call, Okafor and Lind. On call means ready to come in if a patient needs them, and the rule says at least one of them stays on call. Both feel ill on the same evening and press "go off call" within a second of each other. Each press runs a transaction, a group of statements that the database applies together or not at all. Each does what looks safe: count the doctors on call, and leave only if someone else stays.

BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND on_call;     -- 2: someone else stays
UPDATE on_call SET on_call = false WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND doctor = 'Okafor';
COMMIT;

Lind's transaction runs the same statements with her own name. The first line sets the isolation level, the setting that decides how much a transaction sees of others running at the same time. At Repeatable Read, each transaction reads from a snapshot: a picture of the committed data, taken at its first statement and kept to the end. Its own changes stay in a private draft until it commits. The stepper plays the two as a timeline.

Both count 2, from snapshots taken before either wrote. Okafor's UPDATE puts a row lock on Okafor's row, a mark that makes any other writer of that row wait. Lind's UPDATE locks Lind's row, so nobody waits. And no row has two writers, so Repeatable Read, which only compares writers of the same row, has nothing to report. Both commit, and nobody is on call.

This is write skew, the race that took Ivy below zero in What a transaction promises. Every write skew has the same three steps:

  1. A query checks a condition over several rows: at least one doctor on call, a total at or above zero.
  2. The program decides on the answer.
  3. Each transaction writes a row the other one didn't write, and together the writes make the check false.

Run one after the other, the second transaction would count 1 and refuse. Run together, they make a state that no order of the two could make. Two flatmates do the same with a rule that one carton of milk always stays in the fridge. Each opens the door, sees two cartons, and takes one. They took different cartons, so neither saw a clash.

The first fix borrows the lock from Lost updates: lock what the decision reads, not only what it writes. At Read Committed, the default level, which takes a fresh snapshot for each statement, SELECT doctor FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND on_call FOR UPDATE reads both on-call rows and locks them, as an UPDATE would, before the count. Lind's request waits until Okafor's transaction commits. PostgreSQL then rechecks each row against the WHERE part. It drops Okafor, who is now off call, and returns Lind alone: one doctor, so Lind's transaction refuses. This works because the rows the rule reads exist and can be locked. Next, a rule where they don't.

try.title: Empty the shift, then lock it
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder and run psql, PostgreSQL's program for typing SQL, in both: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A and B. Each is one session, an open connection to the database, like one doctor's phone. Start the database first if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait).

In A, create the rota table and its three doctors (the first two statements). Then run the first block one statement at a time, switching terminals at each comment (-- A or -- B). Before the COMMITs, predict whether either one fails.
Run the second block. B's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE hangs until A commits. Predict which doctors it returns.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course
code.html: -- A: the rota CREATE TABLE on_call (shift_id bigint NOT NULL, doctor text NOT NULL, on_call boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true, PRIMARY KEY (shift_id, doctor)); INSERT INTO on_call VALUES (1201, 'Okafor', true), (1201, 'Lind', true), (1202, 'Ruiz', true); -- 1. both doctors go off call at REPEATABLE READ -- A BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND on_call; -- B BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND on_call; -- A: 2 on call, so Okafor may go UPDATE on_call SET on_call = false WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND doctor = 'Okafor'; -- B: 2 on call, so Lind may go UPDATE on_call SET on_call = false WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND doctor = 'Lind'; -- A COMMIT; -- B COMMIT; -- A SELECT doctor, on_call FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 ORDER BY doctor; UPDATE on_call SET on_call = true; -- 2. lock the on-call rows first, at READ COMMITTED -- A BEGIN; SELECT doctor FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND on_call ORDER BY doctor FOR UPDATE; -- B (waits) \timing on BEGIN; SELECT doctor FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND on_call ORDER BY doctor FOR UPDATE; -- A: two rows came back, so Okafor may go UPDATE on_call SET on_call = false WHERE shift_id = 1201 AND doctor = 'Okafor'; COMMIT; -- B: one row came back, so Lind must stay ROLLBACK; -- A SELECT doctor, on_call FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = 1201 ORDER BY doctor;

try.expect:
In block 1, both counts print 2, both UPDATEs print UPDATE 1 at once, and both COMMITs succeed:

 doctor | on_call
--------+---------
 Lind   | f
 Okafor | f
(2 rows)

Nobody is on call, with no error anywhere. In block 2, B's locking SELECT prints nothing until A commits, then returns one row (your time is however long you took):

 doctor
--------
 Lind
(1 row)

Time: 2309.693 ms (00:02.310)

Okafor's row was locked by A, and once A committed it no longer matched on_call, so PostgreSQL dropped it. Lind sees she is the last one on call. The final SELECT shows Lind t (true) and Okafor f (false). Keep the table: the last Try it drops it.

sections.h: The booking that doesn't exist yet: phantoms
sections.html:
Back to the meeting room from the opening, now room 4. A booking is a row in the table room_bookings. Its during column holds a tstzrange, a range of timestamps, from a start time to an end time. Ranges here are half-open: [12:00,13:00) includes 12:00 but not 13:00, so a booking from 13:00 doesn't overlap it. a && b is true when two ranges overlap. Room 4 is free from 12:00 to 13:00, and the app checks before it inserts the new booking:

BEGIN;
SELECT booking_id FROM room_bookings
WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('2026-12-01 12:00+00', '2026-12-01 13:00+00')
FOR UPDATE;                                      -- 0 rows: the room is free
INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, ..., 'settlement review');
COMMIT;

The FOR UPDATE is the doctors' fix, copied here, and it does nothing. A row lock is a mark on a row that exists. The check found no rows, so it marked none. The second booker's check also finds none, and it doesn't wait either, because neither transaction can see the other's insert until it commits. Both insert, both commit, and 12:30 to 13:00 is booked twice. The figure shows the timeline.

The new booking is a phantom: a row that matches a query's search but was written by another transaction after the query ran. In What a transaction promises, a phantom was a nuisance, a second count in one Read Committed transaction that came out one higher. Here it breaks a rule. Both the check and the write are about a row that doesn't exist yet, so the clash between the two transactions has nothing to attach to. Repeatable Read doesn't help either. A snapshot hides the other booking from your reads, and it doesn't stop the other transaction from inserting it.

The same shape turns up wherever a rule says "no row like this may exist yet":

  • a username or an email address that must be unique;
  • one payout per shop per day (the money the company sends a shop for its sales), or one main card per account;
  • the refunds of a payment, which must not add up to more than the payment, when each refund is a new row;
  • a gift card spent twice, when each spend is recorded as a new row.

Each of them checks that something is missing, then inserts it. A row lock can't protect something that's missing. The next three sections give the clash something to hold on to.

figure.caption: Both transactions search room 4 for bookings that overlap their slot, find none, lock nothing and insert, so 12:30 to 13:00 is booked twice.

try.title: Book room 4 twice
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder and run psql in both: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course. Call them A and B, one for each booker. Start the database first if it isn't running (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait).
In A, create the two tables and the first booking (the first four statements).
Run the block one statement at a time, switching at each comment. Does B's locking SELECT wait for A? Predict the bookings of room 4 at the end.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course
code.html: -- A: rooms and their bookings CREATE TABLE rooms (room_id bigint PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO rooms VALUES (4, 'Ledger'), (7, 'Clearing'); CREATE TABLE room_bookings (booking_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, room_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES rooms, during tstzrange NOT NULL, booked_by text NOT NULL); INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, '[2026-12-01 09:00+00, 2026-12-01 10:00+00)', 'risk team'); -- A: is 12:00-13:00 free? Lock whatever is in the way BEGIN; SELECT booking_id FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('2026-12-01 12:00+00', '2026-12-01 13:00+00') FOR UPDATE; -- B: is 12:30-13:30 free? BEGIN; SELECT booking_id FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('2026-12-01 12:30+00', '2026-12-01 13:30+00') FOR UPDATE; -- A: nothing in the way, so book INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 12:00+00', '2026-12-01 13:00+00'), 'settlement review'); -- B: nothing in the way, so book INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 12:30+00', '2026-12-01 13:30+00'), 'card ops'); -- A COMMIT; -- B COMMIT; SELECT booking_id, during, booked_by FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 ORDER BY lower(during);

try.expect:
Both checks print (0 rows) at once; B never waits. Both INSERTs print INSERT 0 1, and both COMMITs succeed:

 booking_id |                       during                        |     booked_by
------------+-----------------------------------------------------+-------------------
          1 | ["2026-12-01 09:00:00+00","2026-12-01 10:00:00+00") | risk team
          2 | ["2026-12-01 12:00:00+00","2026-12-01 13:00:00+00") | settlement review
          3 | ["2026-12-01 12:30:00+00","2026-12-01 13:30:00+00") | card ops
(3 rows)

Bookings 2 and 3 overlap from 12:30 to 13:00. The FOR UPDATE locked zero rows in both sessions, so it changed nothing. Leave the tables as they are for the next Try it.

video.title: Phantoms: when there is no row to lock

sections.h: Give the clash a row to lock, or let a constraint decide
sections.html:
If the clash has no row, give it one. Every booking of room 4 can first lock room 4's own row in the rooms table, before it checks:

BEGIN;
SELECT name FROM rooms WHERE room_id = 4 FOR UPDATE;     -- the second booker waits here
SELECT count(*) FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && ...;
INSERT ...;
COMMIT;

The room's row always exists. So the second booker's lock request waits until the first commits. Then its count, a new statement at Read Committed with a fresh snapshot, sees the first booking. This is called materializing the conflict: turning a clash over rows that might exist into a lock on a row that does.

When no natural parent row exists, you can create rows for the purpose. Say a room_slots table, with one row per room per 15 minutes for the next six months, which every booking locks before it inserts. Treat that as a last resort. The slot table mixes the database's traffic rules into your data. Every writer has to remember to lock it, and one forgotten path through the code brings the double booking back. A parent row is the cheap version: lock the payment before inserting a refund, the shop before a payout, the account before a card.

Better still, write the rule down so the database enforces it. A rule written into a table is called a constraint, and the database refuses any change that breaks one. For an exact match, it's a UNIQUE constraint, which allows no two rows with the same values in the listed columns. UNIQUE (merchant_id, payout_day) allows one payout per shop per day (the labs call shops merchants), and the course's payment_uid has one too. For overlapping ranges, PostgreSQL has the exclusion constraint, a wider kind of UNIQUE: no two rows may make all the listed comparisons true at once.

ALTER TABLE room_bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_double_booking
    EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&);

That reads: no two rows may have the same room_id and overlapping during. PostgreSQL checks it through an index, a sorted structure that finds rows without reading the whole table. This one is a GiST index, a kind that can search ranges for overlaps. The btree_gist extension lets a plain = on a number sit in that index, and the course database already installs it. PostgreSQL 18 adds temporal keys, keys that understand periods of time. The documentation says UNIQUE (room_id, during WITHOUT OVERLAPS) behaves like the same exclusion constraint, and the course's merchant_fee_schedules table uses one.

A constraint holds when two transactions race, because its check looks at every entry in the index, committed or not. In the Try it, B's insert finds A's uncommitted booking, waits for A's transaction, and fails with SQLSTATE 23P01 the moment A commits. (A SQLSTATE is the five-character code PostgreSQL attaches to every error.) There's no check query to get wrong, and no path through the code that can forget it.

If the rule fits a constraint, make it one. The rules that don't fit involve arithmetic across rows: a total, "at least one doctor", a sum of refunds. Next, we'll see how a database can lock a search itself.

try.title: Let the database refuse the overlap
steps: Use the two psql sessions and the tables from the last Try it.
In A, delete the double booking and add the exclusion constraint. Then run the race again with plain INSERTs and no check at all. Predict what B's INSERT does, and when.
Finish with two bookings that should be allowed: back to back in room 4, and the same time in room 7.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course
code.html: -- A DELETE FROM room_bookings WHERE booking_id = 3; ALTER TABLE room_bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_double_booking EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&); BEGIN; INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 15:00+00', '2026-12-01 16:00+00'), 'payroll'); -- B (waits) \timing on BEGIN; INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 15:30+00', '2026-12-01 16:30+00'), 'fraud ops'); -- A COMMIT; -- B \echo :SQLSTATE ROLLBACK; INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 16:00+00', '2026-12-01 17:00+00'), 'fraud ops'); INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (7, tstzrange('2026-12-01 15:30+00', '2026-12-01 16:30+00'), 'fraud ops');

try.expect:
B's INSERT prints nothing while A's transaction is open. It's waiting for A, though nothing locked a row. When A commits (your time differs):

Time: 1906.597 ms (00:01.907)
ERROR:  conflicting key value violates exclusion constraint "no_double_booking"
DETAIL:  Key (room_id, during)=(4, ["2026-12-01 15:30:00+00","2026-12-01 16:30:00+00")) conflicts with existing key (room_id, during)=(4, ["2026-12-01 15:00:00+00","2026-12-01 16:00:00+00")).
23P01

If A had rolled back instead, B's insert would have gone through. The two last INSERTs both print INSERT 0 1: 16:00 to 17:00 starts as payroll's booking ends, and room 7 is a different room. Keep the tables for the last Try it.

aside.title: Why not lock the whole table?
aside.html: LOCK TABLE room_bookings would stop the double booking: every booker would wait for every other one. That's the trouble with it. A booking of room 7 would wait for a booking of room 4, and an office with a hundred rooms would book them one at a time. The fixes in this lesson keep the waiting to transactions that really clash: the same room, the same payment, the same shift. The lab checks exactly this, and fails a fix that makes room 7 wait for room 4.

sections.h: Locking the search itself: predicate locks and MySQL's next-key locks
sections.html:
The general fix is a lock on the search. A predicate lock belongs to a condition, such as room_id = 4 AND during && [12:00,13:00), rather than to rows. (A predicate is the condition part of a query, its WHERE.) The transaction that searched holds it, and any other transaction that wants to insert or change a row matching the condition must wait. It covers rows that don't exist yet, which is what a phantom needs. Two-phase locking, where every lock is held until commit (lesson 5), becomes serializable once it takes predicate locks for its searches. Serializable means the result always matches some order of running the transactions one after the other.

Checking every write against every condition anyone has searched is slow. So real databases lock something coarser that's quick to check: a stretch of an index. Picture the index as a library catalogue, a sorted list of each row's key and where the row lives. MySQL, another free database, does this at its default level, Repeatable Read; the work happens in InnoDB, the part of MySQL that stores the data. A locking read puts a next-key lock on every index entry it scans: a lock on the entry, plus one on the gap before it. A gap lock does one thing: it stops other transactions from inserting into that gap. An INSERT first asks for a lock on the gap it lands in, called an insert intention lock, and waits if someone else holds a lock there.

In the Try it, A runs the room check with FOR UPDATE against an index on (room_id, starts_at), which sorts bookings by room and then by start time. It returns no rows, and still holds locks: performance_schema.data_locks, MySQL's list of current locks, shows next-key locks on room 4's 09:00 and 14:00 entries. B's booking for 13:30 to 14:00 lands in the gap before 14:00. It waits until it times out, although it overlaps nothing A asked about. A next-key lock covers more than the condition: it locked the whole gap between room 4's 09:00 and 14:00 bookings, because the index can't express "overlaps 12:00 to 13:00". A booking at 15:30 lands in the next gap and goes through, and so does one for room 7. Take the index away and the scan touches every row, so a booking for room 7 waits too.

At Read Committed, InnoDB turns gap locking off for searches and index scans. The MySQL documentation keeps it only for the checks behind foreign keys and duplicate keys. The same check then lets the double booking through, as in PostgreSQL.

PostgreSQL has no gap locks. Its FOR UPDATE locks the rows it returns and nothing else, at every isolation level. It does keep notes much like predicate locks, but only at SERIALIZABLE, and they never make anyone wait. That's the last rung of the ladder.

try.title: Watch InnoDB lock a gap
steps: From the labs folder, start MySQL 8.4: docker compose -f env/mysql.yml up -d --wait. Open three terminals there and run docker compose -f env/mysql.yml exec db mysql course, MySQL's program for typing SQL, in each: A, B and C. The table room_bookings has bookings of room 4 at 09:00 and 14:00 and of room 7 at 10:00, with an index on (room_id, starts_at).

In A, run the check with FOR UPDATE and leave the transaction open. In B, set a 5-second limit on lock waits and try to book 13:30 to 14:00, which doesn't overlap 12:00 to 13:00. While it hangs, list the locks in C.

After B gives up, book 15:30 in room 4 and 12:30 in room 7 from B. Predict which of them wait. Then roll back both, and stop MySQL with docker compose -f env/mysql.yml down -v if you won't need it for lesson 4.

code.title: mysql, three sessions on database course
code.html: -- A: is room 4 free from 12:00 to 13:00? (REPEATABLE READ, the default) START TRANSACTION; SELECT booking_id, starts_at, ends_at FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND starts_at < '2026-12-01 13:00' AND ends_at > '2026-12-01 12:00' FOR UPDATE; -- B: a booking that overlaps nothing A asked about (waits) SET innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 5; START TRANSACTION; INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, starts_at, ends_at, booked_by) VALUES (4, '2026-12-01 13:30', '2026-12-01 14:00', 'payroll'); -- C: who holds what SELECT index_name, lock_mode, lock_status, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks WHERE lock_type = 'RECORD' ORDER BY engine_transaction_id, index_name, lock_data; -- B, after the timeout INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, starts_at, ends_at, booked_by) VALUES (4, '2026-12-01 15:30', '2026-12-01 16:00', 'payroll'); INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, starts_at, ends_at, booked_by) VALUES (7, '2026-12-01 12:30', '2026-12-01 13:30', 'card ops'); ROLLBACK; -- A ROLLBACK;

try.expect:
A's check prints Empty set, and C shows that it holds locks anyway (output trimmed):

+------------+------------------------+-------------+--------------------+
| index_name | lock_mode              | lock_status | lock_data          |
+------------+------------------------+-------------+--------------------+
| PRIMARY    | X,REC_NOT_GAP          | GRANTED     | 1                  |
| room_time  | X                      | GRANTED     | 4, 0x99BB829000, 1 |
| room_time  | X                      | GRANTED     | 4, 0x99BB82E000, 2 |
| room_time  | X,GAP,INSERT_INTENTION | WAITING     | 4, 0x99BB82E000, 2 |
+------------+------------------------+-------------+--------------------+

X on an index entry is a next-key lock, and X,REC_NOT_GAP a lock on the row alone. lock_data is the index key: room 4, the start time in MySQL's binary DATETIME format, and the booking id. So A holds the 09:00 booking (scanned, though it doesn't match ends_at) and the 14:00 booking with the gap before it, and B's insert intention waits on that gap. After 5 seconds B gets ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction. The bookings at 15:30 in room 4 and 12:30 in room 7 both print Query OK, 1 row affected at once: they land in gaps A doesn't hold.

refs.title: MySQL 8.4: InnoDB locking (record, gap, next-key and insert intention locks)

sections.h: Serializable finds the clash for you, and you pay in retries
sections.html:
The last rung needs no idea of which row to lock. Run at SERIALIZABLE, and let the database find the clash. Serializable promises that the result is one that some order of the transactions, one after the other, could have produced. How a database keeps that promise differs, and the difference shows when it's busy.

PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE is Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI, met in What a transaction promises). Every read leaves a note, called a SIREAD lock. The note sits on the rows a query returns, on the index pages a search visits, or on a whole table that was read from start to end. A note on the whole table is how a search that found nothing is remembered. These notes never make anyone wait. When a transaction writes a row that falls under another transaction's notes, PostgreSQL records a read-write dependency: one transaction read something the other then changed. When two such dependencies form a dangerous chain, it aborts a transaction with 40001.

In the Try it, both bookers count 0, both insert, A commits, and B's COMMIT fails with could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions. B's retry counts 1 and refuses. The doctors work the same way. The price is the retry loop from What a transaction promises, plus false alarms. room_bookings has no index on room_id, so each count reads the whole table, and two bookings of different rooms can clash too. An index on room_id, or the GiST index behind a constraint, narrows the notes.

MySQL's SERIALIZABLE uses two-phase locking. InnoDB turns each plain SELECT into a locking read with shared next-key locks, which other readers may share but writers must wait for. Both bookers' checks take shared locks on the same gap, and those don't conflict with each other. Then each INSERT needs that gap, and waits for the other: a deadlock, two transactions each waiting for the other forever. InnoDB aborts one with error 1213 (SQLSTATE 40001), and the other insert goes through. That's correct, but every check now blocks writers, and deadlocks become routine.

Oracle Database, a commercial database that many banks run, has no rung here. Its SERIALIZABLE is snapshot isolation, so write skew and phantoms get through, and on Oracle you materialize the conflict or use a constraint. Here is the whole ladder:

Fix Works when What it costs
FOR UPDATE on the rows read the rows exist waiting, and deadlocks if the order varies
lock a parent or slot row one row stands for each conflict every writer must remember to lock it
UNIQUE or exclusion constraint the rule is a key or "no overlap" an index; handle 23505 or 23P01
SERIALIZABLE, PostgreSQL (SSI) any rule retries and false alarms
SERIALIZABLE, MySQL (2PL) any rule blocking and deadlocks

Use a constraint whenever the rule is one. Next, lock a row you can name. Keep SERIALIZABLE for arithmetic across rows you can't name, and give it the retry loop.

try.title: Double-book at SERIALIZABLE
steps: Use the two psql sessions and tables from the earlier Try its.
In A, drop the constraint. Then run the race once more at SERIALIZABLE, with a plain count as the check. Which COMMIT fails? Run B's retry and read its count.

Optional, if MySQL is still up: run the same check and inserts in two mysql sessions after SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; and START TRANSACTION;, using starts_at and ends_at instead of a range. Expect A's INSERT to wait and B's to fail with ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction.

code.title: psql, two sessions on database course
code.html: -- A ALTER TABLE room_bookings DROP CONSTRAINT no_double_booking; BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; SELECT count(*) FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('2026-12-01 13:00+00', '2026-12-01 14:00+00'); -- B BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; SELECT count(*) FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('2026-12-01 13:30+00', '2026-12-01 14:30+00'); -- A: 0, so book INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 13:00+00', '2026-12-01 14:00+00'), 'audit'); -- B: 0, so book INSERT INTO room_bookings (room_id, during, booked_by) VALUES (4, tstzrange('2026-12-01 13:30+00', '2026-12-01 14:30+00'), 'card ops'); -- A COMMIT; -- B COMMIT; \echo :SQLSTATE -- B retries from the start BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; SELECT count(*) FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('2026-12-01 13:30+00', '2026-12-01 14:30+00'); ROLLBACK; -- A: clean up this lesson's tables DROP TABLE room_bookings, rooms, on_call;

try.expect:
Up to A's COMMIT, everything looks like the double booking: both counts are 0 and both INSERTs succeed. Then B's COMMIT fails:

ERROR:  could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
DETAIL:  Reason code: Canceled on identification as a pivot, during commit attempt.
HINT:  The transaction might succeed if retried.
40001

B's insert is rolled back with it. B's retry counts 1, the audit booking, so B refuses. Nobody waited at any point: SSI let both run and threw one away at the end. The last statement drops this lesson's tables.

opening:
Picture the office of the company behind a coffee-shop payments app, with one small meeting room. At 11:58, two teams open the booking app. One books the room from 12:00 to 13:00, the other from 12:30 to 13:30. Both see a free room, and both get "Booked". At 12:30, both teams are at the door.

The app checked before it booked, and it even locked whatever the check found, the fix that worked last time. That's why the double booking is a surprise, and why it's easy to miss. The check found nothing, so it locked nothing.

In Lost updates, two charges to one balance erased each other, and a lock on the row put them in line. Here the clash is with a booking that doesn't exist yet, and you can't lock a row that isn't there. In this lesson, we'll break two rules this way, one about doctors and one about rooms, and climb a ladder of fixes from the cheapest to the most general. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two teams at the door of one meeting room. Each checked that the room was free and locked what it found, which was nothing. The fix was to give the clash something real: the room's own row, a constraint that refuses the overlap, or Serializable with a retry.

When a booking app shows you a free slot, ask what stops someone else from taking it in the same second: a lock on the room, a constraint, or nothing at all.

Next, we'll open up the snapshot this track has leaned on, and find out how a long report can read while payments keep writing, with neither waiting for the other.

compare.title: The same "is room 4 free?" check with FOR UPDATE: PostgreSQL and MySQL

a.label: PostgreSQL 18
a.title: PostgreSQL: row locks only
a.html: BEGIN; -- Read Committed SELECT booking_id FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND during && tstzrange('...12:00', '...13:00') FOR UPDATE; -- 0 rows, 0 locks -- another session inserts 12:30-13:30: no wait -- same at REPEATABLE READ: a snapshot hides the -- new row from you, it does not stop the insert -- the fixes that work here: -- lock rooms WHERE room_id = 4 -- EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, -- during WITH &&) -- SERIALIZABLE: SIREAD locks, never blocking

b.label: MySQL 8.4 InnoDB
b.title: InnoDB: next-key locks at REPEATABLE READ
b.html: START TRANSACTION; -- Repeatable Read SELECT booking_id FROM room_bookings WHERE room_id = 4 AND starts_at < '...13:00' AND ends_at > '...12:00' FOR UPDATE; -- 0 rows, but next-key -- locks on the index -- another session inserts 12:30 or 13:30: waits -- (the gap before room 4's 14:00 entry) -- at READ COMMITTED: no gap locks, no wait -- no usable index: every row scanned is locked -- SERIALIZABLE: plain SELECTs take shared -- next-key locks; two bookers deadlock (1213)

compare.note: The same SQL protects against the phantom on one database and not on the other. InnoDB's locking reads lock the stretches of index they scan, so at MySQL's default level a FOR UPDATE check does block a clashing insert. It also blocks some harmless ones that land in the same gap, and only when an index fits the search. PostgreSQL locks only the rows it returns, and keeps its protection for searches to SERIALIZABLE, where SIREAD notes find the clash at commit instead of blocking. Code written for MySQL's default can lose that protection when it moves to PostgreSQL, or to MySQL at Read Committed, which many teams choose to avoid waits on gap locks.

worked.title: Refunds that never exceed the payment, under concurrency

steps.say: The course schema leaves one rule without a constraint: the refunds of a payment must not add up to more than the payment (a comment on refunds says no CHECK can express it). Payment 5 is 48,000 and already has refunds of 12,000 and 6,000, so 30,000 is left. Two support staff refund 25,000 each at the same moment. Each checks first, at Read Committed:
steps.code: -- 1. the racy version, run by both agents at once BEGIN; SELECT p.amount_minor - coalesce(sum(r.amount_minor), 0) AS refundable FROM payments p LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id WHERE p.payment_id = 5 GROUP BY p.amount_minor; -- 30000 in both sessions: 25000 fits INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (5, 25000, 'customer_request', now()); COMMIT; -- both commit: 68000 refunded on 48000

steps.say: Each refund is a new row, so the check is about rows that don't exist yet: a phantom. No constraint can say "the sum stays under the payment", so materialize the conflict on the parent row, which always exists. Every refund of payment 5 locks payment 5 first:
steps.code: -- 2. one refund of a payment at a time: lock the parent row first BEGIN; SELECT amount_minor FROM payments WHERE payment_id = 5 FOR UPDATE; -- the second agent waits here SELECT coalesce(sum(amount_minor), 0) FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = 5; -- a new statement, so a new snapshot: the second agent sees 43000, refundable 5000 -- insert only if 48000 - sum >= 25000 COMMIT;

steps.say: In Kotlin, the check and the insert sit between the lock and the commit, and every path ends the transaction:
steps.code: // 3. the service method fun refund(conn: Connection, paymentId: Long, amount: Long): Boolean { conn.autoCommit = false try { val paid = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT amount_minor FROM payments WHERE payment_id = ? FOR UPDATE") .use { it.setLong(1, paymentId); it.executeQuery().use { rs -> rs.next(); rs.getLong(1) } } val refunded = conn.prepareStatement("SELECT coalesce(sum(amount_minor), 0) FROM refunds WHERE payment_id = ?") .use { it.setLong(1, paymentId); it.executeQuery().use { rs -> rs.next(); rs.getLong(1) } } if (refunded + amount > paid) { // the rule, checked while we hold the lock conn.rollback() return false } conn.prepareStatement( "INSERT INTO refunds (payment_id, amount_minor, reason, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, 'customer_request', now())", ).use { it.setLong(1, paymentId); it.setLong(2, amount); it.executeUpdate() } conn.commit() // releases the lock: the next refund may check return true } catch (e: SQLException) { conn.rollback() throw e } }

steps.say: The other correct version drops the lock and runs the same reads and insert at SERIALIZABLE, inside the serializable retry function from the lab of What a transaction promises. The lock makes refunds of one payment wait in line, which suits a busy row and needs no retries. SERIALIZABLE needs no idea of which row to lock, and pays with an occasional retry.
steps.code: // 4. the same rule without FOR UPDATE: SERIALIZABLE plus a retry of everything val ok = serializable(conn) { _ -> val paid = amountOf(conn, paymentId) // plain SELECTs, no lock val refunded = refundedSoFar(conn, paymentId) if (refunded + amount > paid) false else { insertRefund(conn, paymentId, amount); true } } // the second agent's attempt fails with 40001; its retry sees 43000 and returns false

lab.title: Keep a doctor on call and a room booked once
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. Four of the twelve fail. Each test builds its own on_call, rooms and room_bookings tables (the same as in the Try its, with a third doctor, Haas, off call, and a second shift, 1202) and drops them at the end.

off_call.sql is one transaction that the tests run in two sessions at once, one statement at a time, taking turns. Read the failure: its log lists every statement each session ran. Okafor and Lind both go off call. Lock the rows the rule reads before the UPDATE decides. Doctors on shift 1202 must not wait for shift 1201.

book_room.sql already has a FOR UPDATE on its check, and the double booking still happens. Make two bookings of the same room meet on a row that exists before they check. Bookings of room 7 must not wait for room 4.

no_overlap.sql holds a statement that changes the table's design, which the tests run once and commit. Replace the placeholder with a constraint that refuses overlapping bookings of the same room. The last test inserts with no check at all, from two sessions, and expects the second insert to wait and fail with 23P01.

Run the tests until all twelve pass. Then try BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE; as the only change in a fresh copy of the first two files, and watch the log: the tests retry a 40001 the way your program would.
hints: For off_call.sql, add after BEGIN: SELECT c.doctor FROM on_call c, off_call_request r WHERE c.shift_id = r.shift_id AND c.on_call FOR UPDATE OF c;, and start the transaction at Read Committed (plain BEGIN;). OF c locks only the rota rows, not the row of the temporary table that holds the request.
For book_room.sql, lock the room: SELECT m.room_id FROM rooms m, booking_request r WHERE m.room_id = r.room_id FOR UPDATE OF m;. The FOR UPDATE on bookings can stay or go: it never locked anything.

For no_overlap.sql: ALTER TABLE room_bookings ADD CONSTRAINT room_bookings_no_overlap EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&);. PostgreSQL 18's UNIQUE (room_id, during WITHOUT OVERLAPS) passes too. A plain UNIQUE (room_id) fails the back-to-back test.

drill.title: The fix ladder, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, choose a fix for each rule and write its SQL: (1) at most one payout per shop per day, in payouts (merchant_id, payout_date, ...); (2) no two bookings of a room overlap, in room_bookings (room_id, during tstzrange, ...); (3) every shift keeps at least one doctor on call, in on_call (shift_id, doctor, on_call): the first statement of the transaction; (4) a shop's refunds today stay under 10,000 in total. Then say why FOR UPDATE on the check in (2) isn't enough on PostgreSQL.

answer.html: -- 1. a key: let a constraint refuse the duplicate (23505) ALTER TABLE payouts ADD CONSTRAINT one_payout_per_day UNIQUE (merchant_id, payout_date); -- 2. no overlap: an exclusion constraint (23P01); needs btree_gist for "=" on bigint ALTER TABLE room_bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_double_booking EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&); -- PostgreSQL 18: UNIQUE (room_id, during WITHOUT OVERLAPS) -- 3. the rows exist: lock them before counting (Read Committed) SELECT doctor FROM on_call WHERE shift_id = :shift AND on_call FOR UPDATE; -- 4. a sum over rows that don't exist yet: lock the parent row first, -- or run at SERIALIZABLE and retry the whole transaction on 40001 SELECT 1 FROM merchants WHERE merchant_id = :merchant FOR UPDATE; -- Why not FOR UPDATE in (2): it locks the rows the check returns. A free -- slot returns none, so it locks none, and a concurrent insert does not wait.

recap: Write skew: two transactions check a rule over the same rows, then each writes a different row, and together they break the rule. Row locks and Repeatable Read don't see it, because no row has two writers.
If the rows the rule reads exist, lock them with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before deciding, at Read Committed. That keeps a doctor on call.
A phantom is a row that matches a search but is inserted by another transaction after the search ran. When the check looks for something missing, FOR UPDATE locks nothing, and both inserts commit.

Give the clash a row (lock a parent row, or a slot table as a last resort), or write the rule as a constraint: UNIQUE for exact matches, EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&) or PostgreSQL 18's WITHOUT OVERLAPS for ranges.

Predicate locks lock the search itself. MySQL's InnoDB comes close with next-key and gap locks at Repeatable Read, through an index, and blocks some harmless inserts too; at Read Committed it takes none. PostgreSQL has no gap locks.

The limit: SERIALIZABLE catches all of these, at a price. PostgreSQL's SSI never blocks but aborts with 40001, sometimes by false alarm, so it needs the retry loop; MySQL's two-phase locking blocks and deadlocks (1213); Oracle's SERIALIZABLE catches neither race.

explain.prompt: A friend added FOR UPDATE to the query that asks "has this shop been paid today?", and says two copies of the program can no longer pay the same shop twice. Explain when that's wrong on PostgreSQL, why it might look right on MySQL, and what you would do instead.
explain.answer: On PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE locks the rows the query returns. If the shop hasn't been paid today, the query returns nothing, so it locks nothing. The second copy's identical query also returns nothing and doesn't wait, neither can see the other's uncommitted payout, and both insert. That's a phantom: the clash is about a row that doesn't exist yet. On MySQL at its default Repeatable Read, the same query takes next-key locks on the stretch of index it scans. If an index fits the search, the second copy's insert waits, and it can look fixed. It stops working at Read Committed or without a fitting index, and it blocks harmless inserts that land in the same gap. The rule "one payout per shop per day" is an exact match, so I'd make it a constraint: UNIQUE (merchant_id, payout_date). The second insert then waits for the first transaction and fails with 23505, which the code treats as "already paid". If the rule were a sum, such as a daily limit, I'd lock the shop's row before reading the total, or run the transaction at SERIALIZABLE on PostgreSQL and retry the whole of it.

deeper.html:
The names in the research papers. Berenson and colleagues' 1995 critique of the ANSI isolation levels named write skew (A5B) when they defined snapshot isolation, and showed that snapshot isolation allows it. Adya's later definitions, in terms of cycles of dependencies, split it in two, and the Hermitage test suite uses his codes. G2-item is write skew where the reads were of particular rows (the doctors). G2 is the general case, where a read was a predicate, a search that might match rows that don't exist yet (the meeting rooms). PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read allows both, and its SERIALIZABLE prevents both.

How a search that found nothing is remembered. Ports and Grittner's paper on SSI in PostgreSQL describes SIREAD locks on rows, on B-tree index pages (which stand for the gaps between keys), and on whole tables. A transaction that holds too many fine-grained locks has them promoted to a coarser level to bound memory (max_pred_locks_per_transaction and friends), which raises false alarms. That's why the PostgreSQL documentation advises plans that use indexes for serializable workloads.

Slot tables, done well. If you must materialize a conflict with no natural parent, create the rows ahead of time (a nightly job adds the next day's slots). Lock them in a fixed order, by slot start, so that bookings spanning several slots can't deadlock. And keep the slot table out of every query except the lock.

Oracle has no exclusion constraint. On Oracle, a "no overlap" rule needs a lock on a parent row, a slot table, or a design where the clash becomes an exact match that a unique key can catch.

A read-only transaction can matter too. Fekete and colleagues describe an anomaly under snapshot isolation that needs three transactions, one of them read-only. A report that reads a closed batch can miss a receipt that a slow transaction adds to that batch afterwards. PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE catches it; Repeatable Read doesn't. Ports and Grittner walk through it with a batch-receipts example.

The book. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 8, covers write skew, phantoms and materializing conflicts in the same order, and is worth reading after this lesson for its framing of serializability.
